blocks.x: This is an interview on the 16th of January 1961 with Charles Hardy, who was born in New Orleans and who plays string instruments. And I've asked him to recall some of his earliest years. When were you born, Charles?
September the 4th, 1895.
And what part of New Orleans were you born in?
I was born down in the old French Quarter.
Did you live there for any considerable time?
Well, we lived there until I was about seven years old. Then we moved, finally moved to Nashville, Tennessee.
Do you remember any music around the French Quarter before you left?

No. I wasn't old enough to even think in terms of music in those days. Yeah. And the reason why we had to leave New Orleans is because my father's business is connected with the various southern properties of the company with whom he was associated. What company was it? The American Cities Company. What kind of property did they have? Which was a company as a subsidiary of the Electric Bond and Share Company in Chicago.
When you say properties, do you mean real estate?
Electric light, power, and real estate. Uh-huh.
You moved to Nashville, and how long were you there?
We were only there a year and a half. Then where? Then we moved to Little Rock. Uh-huh. And from Little Rock we moved to Memphis, and then we moved back to New Orleans.
How old were you when you returned?
We were about, I was eleven years old, New Orleans. And then shortly after that we moved to New York, the main officer of Fort Begdon Davis, who were my father's employers.
When did you take up a hot ukulele?

Well, it's a strange thing. My father's brother married and went to Honolulu on his honeymoon. And he saw these little bitty ukuleles and had these boys strumming on and so forth, and he decided to buy one and bring it back with him. He didn't know anything at all about playing music of any kind. When he did come back, he was wondering who to give it to, and for some reason or rather he handed it to me. Yeah. And that was the beginning of my musical education when he handed me this.
I remember in the twenties that the ukulele was pretty popular around university campuses, but it seems to me they had just come in.
I had mine from 1914.
Yeah.
I think I had one of the first ukuleles in the country.
Was it new to you then? Oh, it was new to everyone.

Nobody knew how to tune it. Oh. So friends of mine that I was just strumming with and playing with occasionally decided that it would be a good idea to tune it as the first four strings on a guitar for easy fingering, which I did. And it proved to be the answer.
Did you have formal lessons?
No. Not in any kind of description.
You depended on your ear, largely?
I depended entirely upon getting chords from friends of mine to play the guitar. Yeah.
Did you study it intensively or did you just kind of come on you?

Oh, I really boned on it. I mean, I tried my best to learn all there was to know about it, even in the early days before the First World War. And strangely enough, at that time, there were quite a number of boys that I went to school with that played various musical instruments. And it was in those early days that the 678s band was formed, which I was a member of.
In New Orleans?
In New Orleans.
Who were some of the boys in that first group that you knew?
The first group that we had was composed of Dr. Edmond Souchon and Bob and Harry Reynolds and Shields O'Ranagan and Bernie Shields and Harrison, Midget Harrison and Roland Rorschach.
Are the instruments that they played, are they well known, you suppose? Otherwise, I think it would be a good idea to mention.

Well, we had two violinists really, Ray Shack and and Midget Harrison. And we had a mandolin player. We had a tenor mandolin player. Who was the tenor? Shields O'Ranagan. And who was the mandolin? Harry Reynolds. And then Souchon was the guitar, and I played the ukulele. I made the seven pieces. And the reason it was the six and seven eighths was because Harrison was only five foot two, and all the rest was about five foot nine or ten. So we called ourselves the six and seven eighths.
It didn't have anything to do with a hat size then?
No, not at all. Man size.
Where were you boys in school at that time?

Well, we all went to the local high school for a year or two, and the third and fourth years of my high school education was spent at Manual Training School, which is Dr. Souchon and Gibbons attended as well. Then, of course, after getting out of high school, we all went to Tulane.
You were all in Tulane and playing together? Yes. When, uh, where'd you begin to get jobs? Do you remember a first job?
First job of what type do you mean?
Playing publicly.

Oh, we didn't, we had no, uh, uh, professional jobs at any time. What we used to do was that, uh, in our college life there were a lot of sororities and fraternities, and they'd give dances in their own houses, at which time we would be invited to play. And our compensation was ice cream and cake in those days.
Well, uh, were you treated as guests? Could you bring a girl or...
Sure, sure. We could leave the band and go dance on the floor and come back and take up an instrument. One of the other boys would get up and dance. It was very interesting.
Did they ever, uh, use alternate bands, or were you the only...
No. Whenever we were engaged to play, when we were engaged, I'd say we were asked to play, and we did it charitably. We didn't expect, expect or take any pay from our services.
And, uh, and you weren't playing ump with another band?
No, no. Not at any time.

Well, at 6th and 7th we've heard some of their more recent records, of course, and, uh, I mean records in more recent years, and, uh, they, uh, as I remember, as an awfully soft group, you'd have to play inside the circle of the band in order to really get the beat. Were you able to deliver enough sound for an instrument?

It's strange, though. Uh, with the combination of instruments that we had, uh, we could play a tune, and it would be, it would sound just like a regular band. When we got the resonances and everything else in it. It was, it's a shame that in those days we didn't have a bass fiddle playing with us. Which later on we acquired, and added considerable to the volume.

Uh, not that the volume was necessary, because I've, uh, noticed that dancers adjust themselves to the volume. That's right, yeah. And, uh, you fellows had, uh, the responsibility of playing a dance beat. Do you think that that helped at all in your acquiring a jazz feel?

Well, we were more or less all inclined in that direction. We had, I don't know why, whether you're born with it down there or not, but, uh, being exposed to so much of it by the professionals that played it, we tried to emulate them.
Yes. Do you remember any of the professionals that you were, uh, especially interested in?

Well, I can remember the first people, uh, with whom I was in contact, was, uh, Piron, who played at the, uh, uh, out of Spanish Fort New Orleans. He, there's a, a supper club out there that he played at all the time, and he was one of the favorites in New Orleans. As well as Robichaux, who used to play at the Louisiana, a restaurant down on Bourbon Street.
How big a band did, uh, uh, you remember, uh, those being?
Well, I can remember there was a, there was seven to eight pieces in those bands at the time. Not any more than that.
Uh, conventionally they used a violin, rhythm section, and some brass?
Yes. Yes.
And then might have a clarinet.
That's right. That's right.

Uh, I, I'm quite sure that the, uh, stories of, uh, those bands are fairly well known, and, uh, uh, Sushan has on many occasions mentioned those two bands. As, uh, uh, school, uh, school boys, you got into these clubs and, and danced to them or heard them?
Yes, we did.
Did you hear any of the rougher music in the French Quarter?

Oh, yes. We used to go down there and, uh, work some kind of a riffle to get into some of those cafes, and we were, not yet old enough, to really be permitted to go, to get into the place. But by hook or crook, we got in there to listen to some of those fellows, and, uh, it added to our knowledge, and our endeavor to emulate, if you know what I mean.
Sure, sure. Well, there were some string players who, uh, later became a prominent. Did you know Johnny Fincere in those years?
I heard of him. I didn't know him personally.
Oh. Or, uh, Bud Scott?
Yes, I've heard of him, too.
But, uh, if, if you heard them, you didn't know them by name? No. Do you remember any of the horn players? Piano players?

Well, in those days, uh, I think that the boys that we played with will remember Erwin LeClaire. I don't think that Erwin ever really followed his music, as well as, uh, Leonard Beisdorfer and, uh, Joe Virgis. Uh, Joe Virgis had composed some tunes in his day, and he was quite a well-known pianist, as well as Beisdorfer. They played mostly, they played mostly the cabarets.
There was a Beisdorfer who, uh, played, uh, trumpets. Was he related?
It may have been. I didn't know him. But I knew Leonard Beisdorfer was a pianist, and he was a good one.
Are these, uh, white or colored boys?
White.
Uh, did they play theaters?
No. No. They played cabarets. Mostly.
Um, uh, Tony Jackson may have been a prominent, uh, party pianist then. Have you heard him there? No. Or Kelly Rowell?
No.
Uh, this, uh, period you're talking about was around 1912, 14?
1912 and 13 and 14. That's right.
Uh, when did you then leave New Orleans?

Well, I belonged to a Washington artillery, which was the National Guard out there, and in 1916, the National Guard out there was assembled and sent to the Mexican border. And, uh, in this battery sea, which I belonged to, were five string music players. So, we continued out playing music while we were on the Mexican border.
Yeah. Do you recall who they were?
Well, there was Souchon, and there was Kleppinger, and there was a Sherman Pardue.
What did Sherman play?
Sherman Pardue played the guitar. And, uh, Bill Gibbons and myself, his father.
And Gibbons was?
Yes.
What was his, uh?
He was a tenor, mandolin.
Uh, now you were playing very much the same kind of repertoire and same performance that you had a little earlier.
That's right.
That's right.
That's right. We just kept trying to keep our hand in. That was all.
Yeah.
And, of course, we were the toasts of the battery when we'd get together and play music, and everybody would really crowd around us and give us a hand when we finished, as you know.
Uh, and where did you go from there?

Well, we left the Mexican border in February of 1917. We came back to New Orleans and were mustered out within ten days. But on April the 7th, if you recall, we were mustered right back into the service for World War Number One. And then the thing really broke up. All points of the compass these boys were sent. So there was no real music playing at all until after the war was over, the First World War, which was 1919. So for two years you were completely... For a few years you were completely... For two years and a half, I would say, there was absolutely nothing in the way of us continuing our music.
Where did you go?

In the war? Yes. Well, I was stationed at... I went to... I was a graduated enlisted man from the Leon Springs Training Camp and Artillery and graduated from the Saumura Artillery School. And at the time of my graduation, there was an urgent need for aerial observers in the Air Force, which was known as a signal call in those days. And I applied for it and passed the examination and became an aerial observer.
What did an aerial observer do? Go up in a balloon? No.
We flew in planes. Oh.
Oh.

And our work was to contact the ground troops and let them know what position our line was with reference to any kind of an advance that they would want to make. We were also required to take photographs of various sections of the front lines. We were also required to strafe the enemy at times, which was the assignment very few of us like to have, if you know what I mean. Yes.
You were not the pilot, however. No.
I was the observed.
You did all the auxiliary work. Did you communicate by phone or...?

No, we communicate by Morse code. Uh-huh. There was no telephones. There was no, in those days, parachutes. If you had to make a landing, you landed with a plane. If you were shot in the air and your wing was damaged and you were coming down, there was nothing for you to do but just hope and pray you'd be alive when the thing hit. Because there was no parachutes in those days.
Did you get into a battle activity?
Yes. I was in the battle area for about three months before the armistice was signed. I finished up with the 168th observation squadron at Manonville, France.
How many trips did this take? How many flights?
I had altogether over the lines about 42 hours, which is a long time.
Did they figure it on an hour flight or a two hour flight?
Everything was based on from when you took off until you landed. How many hours or minutes you were in the air.
It was then limited the gas capacity for the air and so forth and that thing. And does that usually amount to try to get in two hours a day or...?
At the most. Uh-huh. At the most.
Well, that's a lot of flights then. Yes. You're in the military, going back to your graduation, did you come upon any music that you remembered? No.

I can't remember. Except the Rainbow Division put on a big show right after the war in France. That's the 42nd Division of New York. They had a lot of semi-actors from off of Broadway and so forth that put on a show, you know, for all the troops. But it wasn't instrument music. It was sort of a comedy act, you know what I mean? Yes. But I ran into no individual with whom I could collaborate in music at all during the First World War.
Most of the divisions had their own band, but they were military.
Military bands, yes.
One of the Chicago men, a drummer, unfortunately I can't remember his name, but he said that they sometimes played for the civilians in France. Now that was probably after the war.
That's probably so, yes.
If I recall, or rather I don't recall, that any dance music was played for the men as in the Second World War.

That I can't tell you because I didn't hear any of them. I didn't hear any. I wasn't in a position where I would hear them. But I did serve in the services in the Second World War as well. Although I wasn't in uniform.
Well, you mentioned having, in an earlier conversation that we had, that you'd stopped off in New York and heard some New Orleans music in New York.

Yes. And during the First World War, when I, before I went overseas in the First World War, we had heard that there was a tremendous New Orleans jazz band at Rising Webbers in New York. That's on 8th Avenue, just south of Columbus Circle. And, uh, on one, uh, weekend pass, about eight or ten of the boys from, uh, the, uh, Invocation Quarter located at New Jersey went into New York and had something to eat and then went to Rising Webbers. And we heard music like we really loved to hear. It sounded like we were back home in New Orleans.
You'd heard the same type of performance in New Orleans. Oh, yeah.
Same music and everything. We heard it.
Same tunes?

Same, well, mostly the same tunes. And the tunes in those days, they were very popular with high society, for one. And the Muskrat Ramble. And, uh, Rampart Street Parade. And such music as that, that, uh, that really brings out the jazz, the Dixieland jazz, that we know so well and love so well down there.

Uh, I think Rampart Street Parade, at least the title to it, came in a little later. If I remember, the Bob Crosby band was the first to record it, and, uh, it was certainly music typical of New Orleans. That's right. But maybe that title, uh, was affixed later to the theme. That's right. Um, do you remember that they played such things as the Skelet and Jungle, or, uh, Eccentric, or, uh,

Never, don't remember any of those. There's quite a number of other tunes that they were playing. Yeah, well, I think that they're the composition of some of those. Oceana Roll, was one of them. Oh, yeah.
Do you remember?
Yes.
They played that. Do you remember any popular tunes that were used?

Well, another tune in those days was, uh, uh, they could get some real harmony on, was, uh, Fiddle Up, on your violin. No. Lay right on it, rest your chin upon it. Oh, man, that was real music. They really, they knocked that one off, too. Wonderly. Uh, the band you heard is Rides and Webbers. Do you recall an instrumentation? Well, I can recall, it was typically a Dixieland jazz instrumentation. It was a trombone and a trumpet and a clarinet, and, of course, the band, and, of course, the band, a bass fiddle, and, uh, I think it was a tenor sax and a piano. Wow.
The original Dixieland jazz band got to New York after having been to Chicago, but who did you think was the, uh, what did you think was the name of this band?
At that time, I was, I was told it was the Fisher Brothers, the Dixieland jazz band.
Well, we'll have to check that, because, uh, it's possible that a band by the name of Fisher Brothers did play about the same time as the original Dixieland jazz band.
If I don't, uh, mistake it, I think there was a marquee on the outside of the thing. Fisher Brothers with the original Dixieland jazz band.
Is it possible that Fisher Brothers might have been entertainers who were...
No, no, no. There wasn't any entertainment at this place. There was just music and dancing. Uh-huh. And, uh...
And, uh, Fisher Brothers wasn't an alternating band? No. Or in another room?
No.
You think that Fisher Brothers might have been part of the name of the band?
That's right.
Uh-huh. Uh, did you have occasion to talk to the fellas, or tell them that you were from New Orleans?
Yeah, I told them. And they said, that's fine. How's everything on the old hometown?

Uh-huh. Uh, after the success of the original Dixieland jazz band, there were several bands that represented themselves. As, uh, the original Dixieland jazz band. Well, not necessarily using the name, because maybe that was protected legally, I'm not sure. But, uh, there were several that represented themselves as being New Orleans-style bands. Uh-huh. Did you have a chance to hear anybody like Ted Lewis, or, uh...
Oh, yes, I've heard Ted Lewis in the past.
Or emphasize in the same period?
Yes, I think I did. I think I did. If it wasn't, if it wasn't before we went over, shortly after we came back, I heard Ted Lewis.
Uh, was there anything of New Orleans structure in there?

I didn't think so. I really didn't. There wasn't, it didn't have, there's a certain something that a band has to have to register with you, from the standpoint of associating it with New Orleans music. Now, Bob Crosby's band had it, in no uncertain terms. He had it. Dre Badouk, the drummer, you know, and some of the other boys that played in that band were recognized to be, uh, imbued with that, uh, uh, New Orleans's touch, if you know what I mean.
How long were you around New York on your return?
I was in New York from, um, May 5th, 1919, until about the 22nd of May.
Well, not long enough to do an awful lot of...

No, not too much, no. Um... I was anxious to get home, too. I'd been away from home, you might say, for three years, because I was only out of the service about two and a half weeks in New Orleans before I was mustered right back in again.
Uh, the, uh, by home you mean New Orleans, huh? Yes. You went back to New Orleans then?
Oh, yes, yes.
Uh, anybody, uh, you recall, upon your return, who impressed you in music, playing jazz around the world?

In New Orleans? Well, I took up where we left off. Uh, Pierron was still playing, and Robichell was still playing, and they had King Oliver, if you remember him. He was playing that, man. We attended a lot of the musical extravaganzas he put on. And then there was a band, I don't know what the name of it was, but there was a particular, uh, cornetist that had a pop eye. His right eye popped way out of his head and used to call him Monocle. And he had a band of five pieces. And they really did play music, that Monocle group, they really, they used to play a lot of the Tulane gym dancers. That wasn't Oliver? No.
Oliver was, had a, uh, a bad eye, but not, uh, this. Um, now, on your return, you didn't hear any more dances at Tulane, did you? Or, or did you have occasion to go to Tulane?
No, no, that, uh, we had, uh, grown there. That's right.
Prior to the war that you heard the Tulane band. Yes, right. Uh, Oliver, uh, went to Chicago shortly, and I wonder if you heard Oliver before you went to Europe, or after?
When did he come back from Europe?
Well, after you came back in 1919. Yeah.

I think it was, I think it was after we came back, because I think he left about three or four months after I got back from New Orleans to go to Chicago. So I got to pick it back from New Orleans in May, and if I'm not mistaken, he left sometime in September to go to Chicago. Hmm.
Then, uh, how long were you around New Orleans from 1919?

Well, I was in New Orleans from 1919 until 1920, a year, and then I went out to Pacific Coast and joined my father's firm as an engineer, which I had studied at school, but had not graduated as, because of the war. I spent a year out in California, and went back to New York to collaborate in a report we made for the Standard Oil Company problems. And then when that was through, they, they told me that the officers that they were sending a crew, which I was supposed to go with, to Athens, Greece. And I'd just come back from over on the other side, and I didn't want any part of it anymore, so I went home. And I stuck around New Orleans for about four or five months, and friends of mine that I've known, and fraternity brothers, decided to go to Texas oil fields and make a fortune, which we didn't make. And I came back to New Orleans, and, uh, heard from another friend of mine in Peoria, Illinois, that he was in, he was engaged in a business that he liked to have me join up, and I went up and saw him, and decided to go into business with him. And it's a business in which I'm presently engaged in.
Is that, for that long you've been? Yeah. That would have been the early twenties.
Uh, you mentioned the West Coast. Anybody there that impressed you as New Orleans-style musician?
No. I didn't hear anything out there.
What part of the West Coast were you in?

I was, um, most of the time in San Francisco. Uh-huh. And, uh, did some work for the, uh, firm in, uh, the southern oil fields of California, around, uh, New Hall, and, uh, the Murphy Coyote, uh, leases, and Los Angeles and Bakersfield.
When you returned, uh, to, uh, New Orleans on occasion, uh, the six and seven eighths, or, uh, a, uh, at least the nucleus was still active, right? Yes, it was.
And even now we have five members of the old six and seven eighths that still play together.
And the, the annual trip you, uh, take down there, you meditate there?
We always manage to get in a couple of nights of music when I'm down there. Good. We have a lot of fun.
Uh, twenty-five then, uh, up to, uh, uh, Peoria. Does that, uh, kind of end your, uh, intimate contact with New Orleans, uh, men, uh, in the north?

I would say that from twenty-five up to now, uh, my contact with the friends that I had made in New Orleans was severed, except for yearly visits that I made down. Um, I managed to maintain my contact with them only on a yearly basis.
Do you hear any, uh, New Orleans music in these intervening years? Uh, you mentioned the Bobcats. Any others that, uh, have impressed you as carrying the, uh, the, uh, award of New Orleans?

Yes, there's one bunch of boys that I saw grow up from babyhood, and I refer to the Dukes of Dixieland. Uh, those boys, uh, Fred and Frankie, uh, Sinto, uh, uh, no doubt created a very, uh, strong following for themselves and a reputation that's to be envy. They do have a fine band. They play wonderful music, and it's definitely New Orleans Dixieland.
Uh, I see Wingy Manon on occasion. Who? Wingy Manon.
I don't know.

Well, he played around Chicago for a considerable time, usually using Chicago men, but since he's from New Orleans, it was a New Orleans type band. He was the leader, and I steered it into New Orleans channels. Um, there have been, we've had on occasion, several New Orleans bands visiting Chicago for a short time.
Uh, the Owls? Well, I don't know.
Do you recall that the Owls ever came to Chicago?
I don't know. I knew the Owls, and I knew their composition, more or less. Yeah.
Yeah.
And, uh, of course there's three or four members of the Owls now that have long since died. Uh, friends of mine that I knew from high school. So you knew the Owls in New Orleans.
Yeah. Where were they working when you knew them?
They were working at various little spots around town, but they were more professional. Uh-huh. See, the 6th and 7th and 8th was non-professional. Yeah.

The bands that have come up have been Charky's, for example. He played at Hotels on the National Club. That's right. And, uh, I wondered if you'd run, if you've heard some, uh, of his, uh, heard Charky on some of his appearances up there?

No, but I did hear him when he used to have that Sunday afternoon jamboree down on Royal Street in New Orleans. And, uh, we've, we've gone down to that a number of times, my wife and I, and Dr. Sushon, his wife, my sister and her husband. And, uh, we enjoyed Charky's music very much. He's, he's one of his own.

Uh, you recall, uh, Lada, Anton Lada. No. He came north, and, uh, his band was reasonably popular, uh, especially for recording purposes, apparently, he was a good entertaining band. And, uh, made, corresponded to the Dukes of Dixieland in his day, entertaining, uh, New Orleans, I think. Um, there was a band in the East, I wondered if you'd ever heard, uh, the Memphis Five.
I think I have heard the Memphis Five, yes. Yeah. Either on a record or someplace or someplace.
Yeah, well, they were popular on records, uh, Phil Napoleon, and something like Miss Maul,
who played with him.
Yeah. And, uh, uh, Jimmy Durante, for a while, had a Dixieland style band. He played the pianist probably.
Yeah.
And, uh, people, New Orleans musicians, such as, uh, Baquet. Baquet, yeah.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh.

Uh, there were, uh, bands in Chicago, uh, prior to 1925, that, uh, were largely New Orleans men, such as the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. Yes, I've heard of them, too. Mm-hmm. You know them by way of record. In, uh, Peoria, there was no New Orleans musicians, to your knowledge? No, not that I knew of.
Did you ever get into Chicago to hear music? Yes. I used to come into Chicago quite often from Peoria, and the place where we used to go most of the time was the Ratzkelle of the Sherman Hotel.

Who was there? I don't remember the name of the band. It's been so long ago. It was been so long ago. It was been so long ago. It was been so long ago. It was been so long ago. It was been so long ago. It was been so long ago. It was been so long ago. It was been so long ago. It was been so long ago. It was been so long ago. It was been so long ago. It was been so long ago. know of New Orleans musicians here now? No, not that I knew of.

Did you ever get into Chicago to hear music? Yes, I used to come into Chicago quite often from Peoria, and the place where we used to go most of the time was the Ratzkeller, the Sherman Hotel. Who was there? I don't remember the name of the band.
Was that the basement place which later became the theater room?
That's right. College Inn? That's College Inn, yes.
In 25 it could have been bands such as George Olson or Ray Miller.
Might have been, but I don't remember what the name was.
